strengths: Novel and well-motivated framework addressing the genuine gap of treating modular two-stage pipelines as black boxes; the residual decomposition enabling stage-wise uncertainty attribution is conceptually clean and practically useful

Solid theoretical contributions including coverage guarantees for separate quantiles (Theorem 1), existence of ideal scaling parameters (Proposition 2), risk-controlled selection via FWER (Theorem 2), and long-run adaptive guarantees (Proposition 3)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with synthetic experiments carefully isolating upstream/downstream/covariate shifts, two real-world datasets with interpretable diagnostics (Figures 12-13 showing how scaling parameters adapt to different shocks), and extensive ablation studies

Clear interpretability benefits: method identifies which pipeline stage drives uncertainty and enables targeted interventions (demonstrated by selective retraining example showing 24.6→25.3 width reduction)
Flexible framework with multiple formulations (separate vs scaled quantiles) and extensions discussed (multi-stage, auxiliary data, φ-mixing sequences)
weaknesses: Severe practical limitation to two-stage models: extension to K stages (Appendix C.4) has exponential complexity in |Λ|, making it impractical for common 3+ stage pipelines; proposed top-k heuristic lacks theoretical justification

Strong intermediate variable observability requirement (x must be observed for all data points) is frequently violated in practice when x is latent, noisy, or delayed; no analysis of robustness to partial/noisy observations

Significant theory-practice gap for main method (Definition 4 scaled quantiles): lacks finite-sample coverage guarantees for arbitrary (a,b); Proposition 2 only shows existence without constructive method; Theorem 2 provides weaker conditional guarantees (coverage ≥ 1-α-τ with probability 1-δ rather than deterministic 1-α)

Excessive conservatism in benign settings: Table 4 shows 0.94-0.98 coverage when targeting 0.90 (IID linear); intervals 15-34% wider than baselines (Tables 4, Figure 3 automobile data); conservatism stems from FWER but limits practical utility, requiring tolerance parameter τ as additional hyperparameter

Limited practical improvements on real data: automobile dataset (Figure 3) shows comparable/wider intervals than ACI despite better coverage; stock dataset shows incremental improvements; benefits primarily manifest on artificial symmetric shifts, while covariate shifts show no advantage over baselines (Appendix D.3.7)

Abstention presented as diagnostic but unvalidated: method produces empty Λ_val under large shifts; no analysis of abstention frequency or correlation with whether retraining is actually necessary; appears to be reframing inability to predict as a feature

Adaptive algorithm components are ad-hoc: SELECTLAMBDA (Appendix B.5) compares recent averages ΔR̄₁ vs R̄₂ without principled justification; adjusting c_t, d_t to expand Λ_val is heuristic; parameter bounds [-η, 1+η] appear arbitrary

High hyperparameter complexity with 8 parameters (α, τ, δ, γ, η, c, d, k) and significant sensitivity: coverage varies from 0.595-0.880 across γ ∈ {0.01, 0.1} (Table 8); no principled guidance for practitioners on setting these a priori

Limited real-world evaluation: only 2 real datasets (both forecasting); no comparison to simple baseline of retraining entire pipeline when coverage drops; missing applications in other domains (classification, anomaly detection)

Exchangeability assumptions weaker than presented: Theorem 2 requires IID calibration but adaptive method uses sliding windows; Section C.2 φ-mixing extension significantly loosens guarantees; practical guarantees weaker for non-exchangeable real data

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: existing conformal methods treat modular pipelines as black boxes, missing opportunities for stage-specific uncertainty attribution and diagnosis
Provides formal coverage guarantees (Theorem 1 for separate quantiles, Theorem 2 for risk-controlled scaling) with extensions to non-exchangeable settings
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including hyperparameter ablations and interpretability visualizations showing how scaling parameters (a,b) adapt to different types of distribution shifts
Clear motivation from real-world applications (supply chain forecasting, stock prediction) with practical diagnostic value
Discusses extensions to multiple upstream models, auxiliary data, and stationary φ-mixing sequences
weaknesses: Critical coverage guarantee concern: Appendix B.1 acknowledges that Q₁₋α({∆R₁}) + Q₁₋α({R₂}) may not upper-bound Q₁₋α({R}), yet this relationship is central to Theorem 1's proof—the paper dismisses this but it raises fundamental questions about coverage reliability
Definition 2's decomposition (∆R₁ = ||y − µ̂₂(x)| − |y − µ̂₂(x̂)||) is indirect: it measures change in downstream error magnitude rather than actual upstream contribution, limiting interpretability

Theorem 2 guarantees coverage only conditional on calibration set (not unconditional) and with tolerance gap (1−α−τ instead of 1−α); Table 5 shows without tolerance the method over-covers, suggesting nominal level isn't achieved without τ > 0
FWER parameter selection lacks principled grid construction; method abstains when Λ_val = ∅ (frequent in Figure 14) yet this is framed as a feature rather than limitation

Adaptive algorithm (SELECTLAMBDA) is heuristic-based with informal decision rules (e.g., 'if ∆R̄₁ > R̄₂, increase a_t') and no theoretical justification; relies on recycled update rule from prior work with additional parameters adjusted without principled justification

Empirical improvements are modest with substantial trade-offs: Table 1 shows 28.88% wider intervals for marginal coverage gains (84.19% vs 72.80% for upstream shift); Figure 3 shows automobile dataset width 21.085 between baselines (15.696 and 31.058) without clear efficiency edge
No advantage on covariate shift (Appendix D.3.7), limiting applicability; method excels only under asymmetric stage-specific shifts

Parameter explosion: γ, η, δ, τ, k, Λ grid resolution, and initial c,d values require tuning with no principled guidance; different (c,d) values used per experiment (c=d=0.01 vs c=0.05,d=0.01) suggesting post-hoc tuning

Limited novelty: residual decomposition is straightforward from triangle inequality; FWER selection from recent work [2,3]; adaptive algorithm largely reuses Gibbs & Candès [14]; multi-stage extension (Appendix C.4) faces exponential complexity making it impractical
Scope limited to two-stage models; extensions to multi-stage are theoretically and computationally problematic

Presentation issues: eight hyperparameters with notation table in Appendix B.2; unclear relationship between Definitions 3 and 4; no algorithm for constructing candidate grid Λ; signed residual alternative (Appendix C.1) performs worse (frequent NA) but shows decomposition choice is not robust

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitation in existing conformal methods: inability to attribute uncertainty to specific pipeline stages or diagnose component failures under asymmetric distribution shifts
Theoretically sound framework with formal coverage guarantees maintained throughout (Theorems 1-2, Proposition 3), properly applying FWER control with super-uniform p-values

Practical diagnostic value: enables practitioners to identify which stage contributes to uncertainty and guides targeted retraining decisions; concrete example shows retraining only upstream achieves comparable gains to full retraining

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: synthetic controlled shifts, two real-world datasets (supply chain, stocks), extensive ablation studies (γ, η, δ, k, τ), clear visualizations of component contributions over time
Honest reporting of negative results including poor performance of signed residual heuristic, absence of advantage under covariate shift, and limitations of DtACI comparison
Extensive documentation supporting reproducibility: detailed algorithms, notation tables, proofs in appendix, experimental hyperparameters clearly specified
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (split conformal, FWER control, adaptive conformal methods) rather than introducing fundamental innovation; core contribution is clever engineering of known tools

Asymmetric benefits across shift types severely limit applicability: clear advantage for upstream concept shifts but no advantage for covariate shifts (Appendix D.3.7), undermining generality claims; efficiency-robustness trade-off shows method is conservative, requiring coverage ≥1-α rather than ≈1-α

Scalability concerns inadequately addressed: multi-stage extension (Appendix C.4) acknowledges exponential growth in search space Λ with heuristic top-k solution lacking theoretical guarantees; multi-upstream models (C.5) suffer same limitation

Limited real-world validation: only two datasets tested; automobile results show modest advantage over ACI (width 21.085 vs 15.696) despite ACI having lower coverage; claims of practical utility would benefit from more domain-specific applications

Restrictive intermediate representation assumption: requires x observable in training, conformal, and calibration sets, significantly limiting applicability compared to black-box conformal methods in practice

Parameter proliferation (8 hyperparameters: a,b,c,d,α,δ,γ,η,τ,k) with insufficient guidance in main text; practitioners lack clear recommendations for default selection; SelectLambda algorithm exhibits heuristic decision rules without strong theoretical justification

Narrow baseline comparisons: only split/adaptive conformal methods tested, no comparison to other modular or staged uncertainty quantification approaches; missing statistical significance tests despite reporting standard deviations

Key design choices insufficiently justified in main text: why decompose residuals vs. work with ∆R₁+R₂ directly? Why use absolute values for ∆R₁? Why FWER over other corrections? These critical choices relegated to appendix discussion

strengths: Novel problem formulation addressing a genuine gap in conformal prediction: stage-wise uncertainty attribution in multi-stage pipelines
Sound theoretical framework with multiple coverage guarantees (Theorems 5.2, 6.1) and extensions to φ-mixing and multi-stage settings
Comprehensive experimental validation across synthetic and real-world datasets with extensive ablation studies and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis
Practical diagnostic value: identifies which pipeline stages drive prediction uncertainty, enabling targeted interventions
Robust coverage under asymmetric stage-wise distribution shifts, demonstrated convincingly on controlled synthetic experiments and real data (automobile supply chain COVID-19 shift)
Methodologically complete with FWER-based parameter selection, adaptive variant with long-run guarantees, and practical hyperparameter guidelines
Well-organized presentation with effective visualizations (e.g., Figures 16-17 showing residual component adaptation) and extensive appendices
weaknesses: Proposition 5.5 establishes existence of ideal scaling parameters (a*, b*) but provides no characterization or construction method; gap between existence and practical FWER selection lacks theoretical elegance

Coverage-efficiency tradeoff inadequately analyzed: method produces unnecessarily wide intervals and frequent abstention (Λval = ∅) under severe shifts; covariate shifts (Section D.4.7) show no advantage over baselines, suggesting specialized applicability
Problem scope limited to two-stage models with observable intermediate representations; multi-stage extension (Definition C.4) faces computational explosion and practical infeasibility
Residual decomposition captures upstream error indirectly through downstream model lens; ∆R₁ doesn't isolate upstream error in nonlinear scenarios; upper bound property R ≤ ∆R₁ + R₂ can be loose
IID assumption on Scal in Theorem 6.1 conflicts with adaptive sliding window approach used in practice; φ-mixing extension (C.2) only sketched
Tolerance parameter τ needed to match baseline efficiency in IID settings (Tables 5) somewhat undermines 'risk-controlled' framing; practical benefits require τ ∈ [0.03, 0.05]

Numerous hyperparameters with somewhat arbitrary defaults (γ=0.01, η=0.01, δ=0.3, k=100) despite ablations; FWER algorithm choice (Bonferroni vs. fixed sequence testing) significantly impacts results but guidance is limited

Real-world automobile experiment shows comparable mean width to baselines (18.957 vs. ACI 15.696) despite claimed robustness; gains appear specialized to stage-wise shifts rather than general distribution shifts

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing an under-explored gap in conformal prediction for modular pipelines
Clear mathematical framework with principled FWER-based calibration and solid coverage guarantees
Comprehensive treatment with extensive experiments, ablations, and theoretical extensions (φ-mixing, multi-stage sketches)
Adaptive method with long-run coverage guarantee and practical guidelines for hyperparameter selection
Intuitive residual decomposition that enables stage-wise error attribution
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core residual decomposition is straightforward extension of Gong et al. (2023), with only incremental improvements (FWER selection, adaptive extension)
Fundamental unresolved tradeoff: FWER calibration is over-conservative (IID coverage 0.9439 vs. target 0.9), requiring tolerance parameter τ that weakens guarantees and adds hyperparameter complexity

Mixed experimental evidence: method produces wider intervals than baselines, over-covers in IID settings, and matches rather than exceeds performance; benefits limited to stage-wise shifts only (covariate shift shows no advantage)
Severe scope limitations: restricted to two-stage models; multi-stage extension faces exponential scaling with set Λ; most modern systems are single-stage or have >>2 stages

Strong and unrealistic assumptions: requires observable intermediate variables (not practical for deep learning pipelines), deterministic symmetric learning algorithms, and IID calibration data despite motivation to handle distribution shifts—this contradiction is unresolved

Theoretical gaps: Proposition 5.5 conditions ('mild regularity') are vague; Theorem 6.1 assumes IID S^cal but requires coverage under shifted test data (connection not rigorously established); exchangeability of ΔR₁ depends on non-standard learning algorithm assumptions
Hyperparameter complexity: method requires tuning α, c, d, a, b, δ, τ, γ, η, k, and Λ grid; guidelines in appendix are largely heuristic with no systematic sensitivity analysis

Experimental limitations: synthetic data uses overly simple linear relationships; non-linear settings explored briefly; no experiments on realistic deep learning pipelines; limited real-world datasets; comparison with cascaded confidence relegated to appendix despite similar performance

Unclear practical behavior: limited empirical analysis of abstention frequency (Λ_val = ∅); no experiments validating core assumption of intermediate variable observability; unclear when proposed method should be used over simpler alternatives
Definition 4.2 (first-stage delta) uses awkward double absolute values without clear justification; over-parameterization without demonstrating it yields better solutions than simpler aggregations

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a real gap in conformal prediction for two-stage pipelines where asymmetric distribution shifts affect stages differently

Clean and intuitive residual decomposition (R ≤ ∆R₁ + R₂) with rigorous theoretical analysis: solid coverage guarantees (Theorems 5.2, 6.1), existence results (Prop. 5.5), and long-run guarantees for adaptive variant (Prop. A.1)

Comprehensive experimental validation across synthetic and real-world datasets with systematic evaluation of shift types (upstream/downstream, gradual/rapid), extensive baseline comparisons, hyperparameter ablations, and single-stage baselines that isolate benefits of two-stage decomposition

Practical diagnostic capabilities enabling practitioners to identify problematic stages via parameter visualization and determine whether targeted retraining is necessary—absent in standard conformal methods

Thoughtful algorithmic design combining FWER control with adaptive parameter updates, preserving formal coverage guarantees while responding to component-wise shifts; parameters provide practitioners with explicit control via flowchart (Appendix D.2)
Black-box access requiring only structural knowledge of pipeline; extension to ϕ-mixing (Section C.2, Corollary C.2) addresses non-IID settings thoughtfully
Well-presented with clear visualizations, consistent notation, and comprehensive appendices documenting hyperparameter guidelines and implementation details
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: residual decomposition is straightforward; FWER control builds directly on Bates et al. (2021) and Angelopoulos et al. (2025); adaptive algorithm largely from Gibbs & Candès (2021). The contribution is combining existing techniques rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts

Highly specialized applicability: benefits are restricted to asymmetric stage-wise shifts. For covariate shifts (D.4.7), the method provides no advantage over baselines while remaining wider. Multi-stage extension (C.4) shows poor scaling (exponential growth in Λ), severely limiting practical scope

Coverage-efficiency trade-offs undermine practical advantages: method over-covers in IID settings (Table 4: 94-98% vs. 90% target), requires τ > 0 to compete with baselines, and often has wider intervals than ACI/PID (e.g., Figure 12: 18.96 vs. 15.70). Method trades efficiency for robustness in specialized regime rather than strictly dominating alternatives

Incomplete treatment of scaled parameters: Proposition 5.5 only establishes existence of ideal (a*,b*), not efficient discovery; no sample complexity analysis for grid size |Λ| relative to |S_cal|; loose upper bound Q₁₋α({∆R₁}) + Q₁₋α({R₂}) contributes to width inefficiency but insufficiently addressed

Theoretical gaps in main algorithm: Theorem 6.1 assumes IID S_cal but adaptive method (Section 7) uses sliding windows violating this; ϕ-mixing extension (C.2) has limited experimental validation (only D.3.4 synthetic AR(1)); no formal analysis of how grid resolution affects coverage guarantees

Experimental concerns: (i) Cascaded Confidence comparison may be unfair—CC's heuristic K-means clustering dismissed while paper's FWER grid search is also somewhat heuristic; (ii) ECI/DtACI designed for online adaptation, not fixed-horizon forecasting, making comparisons less meaningful; (iii) mostly linear synthetic relationships, missing nonlinear scenarios

Hyperparameter complexity: 8+ hyperparameters (α, a, b, c, d, γ, η, δ, τ, k) introduce significant tuning burden despite flowchart; sensitivity analysis (Tables 8-11) shows modest robustness; practitioners must carefully decide when benefits justify added complexity

Presentation: paper is lengthy (37 pages total); main text could be more concise (Sections 5-6 contain redundancy); missing explicit guidance on choosing non-adaptive vs. adaptive variants; informal treatment of how c, d control abstention
